text: Mango Markets needed to know the current price of its listed assets, including its own token MNGO, to figure out how much a trader's position was worth and how much they could safely borrow against it. That number came from a price oracle — a feed sourced from exchanges. The question every protocol has to answer is: how hard is it for one actor to move the exchanges that oracle reads from?

On October 11th, 2022, the attacker opened matching long and short positions in a perpetual swap tied to MNGO, then aggressively bought MNGO on the thin external exchanges feeding Mango's oracle — not on Mango itself. Over about thirty minutes, the oracle-reported price of MNGO rose more than thirteen times over.

Mango's own calculation of his position's value used that same manipulated oracle price, so his long position looked vastly more valuable on paper. With that inflated paper value as collateral, he borrowed essentially every other asset Mango held in its treasury — the CFTC's complaint alleges over $110 million drained this way.

No contract bug was triggered and no function reverted when it shouldn't have — every transaction executed exactly as written. Unlike the flash-loan attack, this used the attacker's own capital, unfolded gradually over thirty minutes, and manipulated markets external to the protocol itself. The fix: bound a position's value by the real liquidity backing it, and require a deviation check against a slower reference price before trusting a large, sudden move.

A price oracle averaging multiple exchanges is only as resistant to manipulation as the combined depth of the markets it's averaging — the deeper issue was that MNGO's real-world liquidity was thin enough for one well-capitalized trader to move it everywhere the oracle looked. Next up: a bug that didn't manipulate any price at all — it froze half a billion dollars without stealing a cent.
